Keeps apart from a8e03: here the answer key sat in the lookup index and was read at question time; nothing was trained. The take-home is an email released at 20:00; no letters. Timeline: Thursday 12 November 2026, the shoe shop's late opening ends at 20:00 and the email arrives; building starts at 21:00; by 01:00 the index holds 300 chunks from 50 documents and eval.csv (20 rows) is written on the desktop; tuning 02:00 to 04:00 on those 20 questions gives 15 right, 17 faithful, recall@5 16 of 20; at 04:30 (Friday 13 November) the tidy moves eval.csv into data/eval/; the 04:40 re-index makes 300 + 20 = 320 chunks; the 05:00 scorer reads 20, 20 and 16 of 20; at 05:10 answer 7's citation, eval.csv row 7, alerts her; she posts at 05:20. Per-question data, all given in the sim: recall misses 4, 9, 13, 16; wrong 4, 9, 13, 16, 18; not faithful 9, 13, 18; each question's own row 0.99, best document chunk 0.70 to 0.85 (question 7: 0.81; question 11: 0.85). Fresh set (warn reply, 05:20 to 07:20, leaving 40 minutes): 13, 16, 15 of 20. Graders' hidden questions: 7 of 10 for every reply. Feedback arrives Tuesday 17 November. title: The Sealed Envelope

post.author: u/late_opening_mererid
post.title: I sell shoes on the late shift and applied for an AI engineer job. At 05:00 my take-home scored 20 of 20, and every answer cited my own answer key.

blocks.text: I'm a sales assistant at a shoe shop. On Thursdays we open late, until 20:00. I've applied for an AI (artificial intelligence) engineer job at a company that builds assistants for shops. Their next step was a task you do alone at home, against a deadline. That's called a take-home.

Mine was released by email at 20:00 on Thursday 12 November, as I counted the till. Due 08:00 Friday: 12 hours. It held 50 documents from a shoe retailer, name removed: size guides, care guides, the returns policy, repair prices. I had to build an assistant that answers questions from them and names the document each answer came from. That's called citing a source.
I also had to write 20 test questions, each with its right answer. A set like that is an eval set.
Then two scores out of 20. First: was the right document among the top 5 pieces it found? That's recall@5. Second: does each answer stick to what was found, adding nothing? That's faithfulness.

blocks.title: Take-home: AI engineer, assistants for shops
items: 50 documents in data/: size guides, care guides, the returns policy, repair prices.
Build a question-and-answer assistant that cites its sources.
Write 20 test questions with reference answers. Report recall@5 and faithfulness on them.
Two pages. We grade your decisions, trade-offs and write-up, not only the score.
We will also run our own hidden questions.

blocks.text: I started at 21:00 at the kitchen table. First the indexer: it reads every file under the data/ folder, cuts each into short pieces called chunks, and stores them ready to search. That job is indexing. By 01:00, 50 documents made 300 chunks.

Each question then runs in three steps. The search scores every chunk for similarity, near 1 when two texts say the same thing, and keeps the top 5. A language model, a program that writes text, answers from those 5. It cites the chunk it used.

At 01:00 I typed my questions and right answers into a table file on my desktop, eval.csv (csv: comma-separated values). That file is my answer key, like the sheet a teacher marks from. I made question 18 unanswerable: the price to resole ski boots. Its right answer is that the documents don't say.

From 02:00 to 04:00 I tuned: I changed the chunk size, the instructions and the search, and after each change ran my scorer, the script that marks each answer against the key. At 04:00, of 20: 15 right, 17 faithful, recall@5 16. Question 18 said '£35', the walking-boot resole price.

At 04:30 I tidied the project for handing in and moved eval.csv into data/eval/. At 04:40 I re-indexed, running the indexer again. At 05:00 I ran the scorer. Each line shows the question, right or not, faithful or not, and the citation.

q01  right  faithful  eval.csv, row 1
q07  right  faithful  eval.csv, row 7
q18  right  faithful  eval.csv, row 18
right 20 of 20  faithful 20 of 20  recall@5 16 of 20

I read the totals, not the last column. At 05:10 I copied answer 7 into my report as an example and saw its citation: eval.csv, row 7. Question 18 now said 'the documents don't say', word for word my key.
My assistant had found the answer sheet, and it answered in my own words.
The indexer's log says 320 chunks: the 300, plus one per row of eval.csv, since it cuts a table by rows. Recall@5 stayed 16 because my recall check ranks only the 300 document chunks.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at your kitchen table is haunted. The model only answers from the chunks the search hands it, and since 04:40 the search could read your answer key. When a test's answers get into the system being tested, that is called leakage: the test leaks into what it measures. And questions you kept changing the system to pass are questions you tuned on; a score on them shows how well you fitted those 20. Two questions. What similarity did question 7's own row score, against its best chunk from the documents? And which five were wrong at 04:00? The take-home round is testing exactly this night.

replies.author: u/late_opening_mererid
replies.text: Question 7's own row: 0.99. Its best document chunk: 0.81. Every question's own row scores 0.99; their best document chunks score 0.70 to 0.85. Wrong at 04:00: 4, 9, 13 and 16, where the search never found the right document, and 18, the £35.

comments.author: u/everyone_tunes_angharad
comments.text: Everyone tunes on their own test set; graders want a high number. Your scorer printed 20 of 20, so hand that in. Don't burn your last hours on a leak check, a little script that hunts your index for your own test questions. Nobody marking a take-home opens your data folder.

replies.author: u/late_opening_mererid
replies.text: The email says they'll also run their own hidden questions.

comments.author: u/bigger_model_blathnaid
comments.text: If 15 of 20 is the honest number, lift it. Switch the assistant to a bigger language model before 08:00. A bigger one usually reads the chunks better, and it's one setting.

replies.author: u/late_opening_mererid
replies.text: It's one setting and then nothing tested. I'd have no time left to score it, or to write about it.

reply.prompt: It's 05:20 on Friday 13 November, and the take-home is due at 08:00. What should I change before I hand it in? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Move the key out, add a leak check, and report 15 of 20 as tuned on.
options.part2: First I added a leak check to the scorer. It fails the run if any chunk comes from the test file, or any test question matches a chunk at a similarity of 0.98 or more. On the 04:40 index it failed: 20 chunks from eval.csv, 20 of 20 questions at 0.99. Then I moved eval.csv to a tests/ folder outside data/ and re-indexed: 300 chunks. The check passed: no chunks from eval.csv, top match 0.85. The scorer read 15 of 20 right, 17 of 20 faithful, recall@5 16 of 20. In the report I labelled them 'questions I tuned on', listed the five failures (4, 9, 13 and 16, where the search missed the right document, and 18, the £35 borrowed from walking boots), told the leak in four lines, and made 'a fresh test set' the first next step. I sent it at 07:40 with a README, the file that says how to run it, which I had run from a clean folder. The feedback came on Tuesday 17 November. On their 10 hidden questions the assistant was right on 7. The reviewer's note said the leak check was what they wanted to talk about.
options.senior: A score is only worth what it was measured on. Keep test data where the system cannot read it, and make that a check that fails loudly, not a habit. Report the honest number with its denominator and say what it was measured on: questions you tuned on flatter the system, so label them and name a fresh set as the next step. Graders read the decisions, the failures and the limits; a 15 of 20 they can trust tells them more than a 20 of 20 they can't.

options.text: Submit 20 of 20 right: the email asks for scores, and the scorer says so.
options.part2: I submitted at 05:30: 20 of 20 right, 20 of 20 faithful, recall@5 16 of 20, with answer 7 as the example, citation and all. The feedback came on Tuesday 17 November. On their 10 hidden questions the assistant was right on 7. The reviewer had opened data/eval/, found eval.csv, and asked one thing: why does every answer to your own questions cite your answer key? In the sim the hidden questions score 7 of 10 wherever eval.csv sits, because none of them is in it. The 20 of 20 measured my key, not my assistant.
options.senior: A system that can read the answer key copies it, so a perfect score with every answer citing the test file is a measurement of the key. Hidden questions, which graders and real users both bring, find the gap at once. Submitting it also tells the reviewer you didn't look at your own outputs, which is the habit a take-home is checking for.

options.text: Drop the numbers and show five strong example answers in the report.
options.part2: I moved eval.csv to a tests/ folder outside data/ so the examples would cite real documents, re-indexed to 300 chunks, and wrote up five answers that came out well: 1, 2, 7, 11 and 15. No scores. The feedback came on Tuesday 17 November. The brief had asked for recall@5 and faithfulness, and the report gave neither, so they couldn't tell whether five good answers were 5 of 6 or 5 of 20. On their 10 hidden questions the assistant was right on 7.
options.senior: Examples show what good looks like; they can't show how often it happens. Chosen examples are the best cases by design. A brief that asks for measures wants counts with denominators, and the failures alongside them, so the reader can judge the system and not the selection.

options.text: Write 20 fresh test questions now and report only the score on those.
options.part2: At 05:20, with 2 hours 40 minutes left, I moved eval.csv to a tests/ folder outside data/, re-indexed to 300 chunks, and started 20 new questions in a new file. Writing them, with their right answers, took until 07:20. On those: 13 of 20 right, 16 of 20 faithful, recall@5 15 of 20. That left 40 minutes for the two pages. The report gave the fresh scores and nothing about the 20 I tuned on, the leak or the failures, and I never ran the README from a clean folder. The feedback came on Tuesday 17 November: the number looked honest, the write-up was thin, and nothing in my code would stop the key leaking next time. On their 10 hidden questions the assistant was right on 7.
options.senior: Questions the system was never tuned on give the cleanest number, and a fresh set is the right next step. But written by a tired author in the last hours, it eats the time the graders actually read: the decisions, the failures, the limits. It also leaves no check in the code, so the same leak can come back. Do it when there's time; at 05:00, the leak check and an honestly labelled report come first.

sim.title: Replay the take-home night
sim.lede: You're the candidate at 20:00 on Thursday 12 November 2026, at the till, before the email arrives. No real model runs here: every similarity and every right, faithful and recall flag is given data. Given: 50 documents under data/ cut into 300 chunks; eval.csv, 20 rows, written at 01:00, which the indexer cuts one row per chunk. For the 20 questions she tuned on (02:00 to 04:00): each question's own eval.csv row scores 0.99; its best document chunk 0.70 to 0.85. The right document is in the top 5 of the 300 document chunks for all but questions 4, 9, 13 and 16. Answered from the documents, questions 4, 9, 13, 16 and 18 are wrong, and 9, 13 and 18 are not faithful; question 18 says '£35'. When eval.csv is indexed, a question takes whichever chunk scores higher and copies it. 20 fresh questions, written 05:20 to 07:20: recall misses 3, 11, 14, 17 and 20; wrong 3, 6, 11, 14, 17, 19 and 20; not faithful 6, 14, 19 and 20; their nearest eval.csv row scores 0.66 or less. The graders' 10 hidden questions: wrong on 3, 7 and 10. The leak check fails if any chunk comes from eval.csv or any question's top chunk scores 0.98 or more.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step the time of night. 01:00: 300 chunks. 04:00: 15, 17 and 16 of 20, and question 18 says £35. 04:30: eval.csv in data/eval/, still 300 chunks. 04:40: 320. 05:00: 20, 20 and still 16, and question 18 copies the key. 05:10: answer 7 cites eval.csv, row 7, with 2 h 50 min left. Turn the leak check on: it fails, 20 chunks and 20 of 20 questions at 0.98 or more. Move eval.csv to tests/: 300 chunks, the check passes at a top match of 0.85, and the scores fall back to 15 and 17. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the kitchen table was haunted. At 04:30 the answer key was moved into the folder the indexer reads, the 04:40 re-index cut it into 20 chunks, and each test question then matched its own row at 0.99, far above any document at 0.70 to 0.85. The model copied the key, so right and faithful read 20 of 20; recall@5 stayed 16 because it ranks only the document chunks. The honest score was 15 of 20, on questions she had tuned on.

steps.title: What the 04:40 re-index did.
steps.text: Indexing runs in three steps. First, the indexer lists every file under data/, whatever its kind. Second, it cuts each file into chunks: documents into short passages, and a table one row per chunk. Third, it stores each chunk, ready to search, with the name of the file it came from. At 01:00 that gave 300 chunks from 50 documents. At 04:40, after the tidy, it found eval.csv in data/eval/ and added its 20 rows: 300 + 20 = 320. What can go wrong: the indexer has no idea which files are test data. Anything placed under data/ becomes something the assistant can find and cite.

steps.title: Why every answer copied the key.
steps.text: Each question runs in three steps: the search scores every chunk for similarity and keeps the top 5, the model answers from those 5, and the answer cites the chunk it used. Each row of eval.csv holds a question word for word with its right answer, so every question matched its own row at 0.99, while its best document chunk scored 0.70 to 0.85. The row came first every time, and the model copied it. That is why question 18 went from a made-up '£35' to 'the documents don't say': the key said so. What can go wrong: the assistant looked better at the exact moment it stopped being tested.

steps.title: Why faithfulness rose and recall@5 didn't.
steps.text: Faithfulness (a5e03) asks whether the answer sticks to what was found. It never asks whether what was found should have been there, so copying the key scored 20 of 20. Her recall@5 check (a5e02) ranks only the 300 chunks cut from the documents and asks whether the right document is in the top 5, so the answer rows never entered it and it stayed 16 of 20. Two measures moved and one didn't, which is itself a clue. What can go wrong: a measure is only as honest as what it can see, so read the citations, not just the totals.

steps.title: Tuned on is not tested on.
steps.text: From 02:00 to 04:00 she changed the system and re-ran the same 20 questions after each change, keeping what helped. Those 20 became questions she tuned on, the way a golden set (a5e01) stops being fair once you adjust to it. 15 of 20 is honest about those questions, but it flatters the system: on questions it has never met it will usually do a little worse. The graders' hidden questions are exactly that: 7 of 10. What can go wrong: a report that doesn't say which questions a number came from invites the reader to assume the best.

steps.title: The take-home as a job: read, plan, check, write.
steps.text: Read the brief for what is graded: here decisions, trade-offs and the write-up, not only the score. Plan the 12 hours in four parts: build, test, write, and a buffer for the thing that goes wrong. Keep test data outside anything indexed, and add a leak check that fails if any chunk comes from the test file or any question matches a chunk at 0.98 or more. Report each number with its denominator and what it was measured on, show the failures, state the limits and the next steps, and ship a README that runs from a clean folder. What can go wrong: the report gets the last hour, and the last hour is the one a leak eats.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: data/ holds only the 50 documents; the index has 300 chunks; eval.csv sits in tests/, outside data/; the leak check passes, with 0 chunks from eval.csv and a top match of 0.85. Bottom row: the scorer reads 15 of 20 right, 17 faithful, recall@5 16 of 20; the label says questions I tuned on; the five failures are shown, questions 4, 9, 13, 16 and 18; the first next step is a fresh test set.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: data/ holds only the documents, the index has 300 chunks, eval.csv lives in tests/ where nothing indexes it, and the leak check compares the two before every scorer run. Bottom row: the honest scores, labelled as questions she tuned on, with the five failures shown and a fresh test set as the first next step.

fix.title: The fix: key out, a leak check that fails loudly, and a labelled report
fix.text: Move eval.csv out of anything the indexer reads, into tests/, and re-index: 300 chunks. Add a leak check to the scorer that fails the run if any chunk comes from the test file, or any test question matches a chunk at a similarity of 0.98 or more; on the 04:40 index it fails at 20 chunks and 20 of 20 questions, and on the new one it passes at a top match of 0.85. Report 15 of 20 right, 17 of 20 faithful and recall@5 16 of 20, labelled 'questions I tuned on'. Show the five failures, say what the numbers don't show, and name a fresh test set, written before any more tuning, as the first next step.

limits: The leak check finds copies, not cousins. A test question reworded in a document, or a near-twin at 0.95, passes it; a8e03 shows that kind of leak in training data.
20 questions is a small set: one answer moves the score by 5 in 100. 15 of 20 and the hidden 7 of 10 agree roughly, and roughly is all 30 questions can say.
A number on questions you tuned on stays flattering however honestly it is labelled. Only questions written before the tuning, and never adjusted to, can say how the system meets new ones.

explain.seniorTake: A take-home tests the work around the system as much as the system: whether you read what is graded, plan the time, measure honestly and say what your numbers mean. The first rule of measuring is that the thing being measured must not be able to see the answers. In a lookup system that means test data never sits anywhere the indexer reads, and a leak check that fails loudly is better than a folder you promise to keep clean. The second rule is to say what each number was measured on. Questions you tuned on give a flattering number; label it, show the failures, and name a fresh set as the next step. A 15 of 20 that the reader can trust, with its five failures explained, is worth more than a 20 of 20 that falls apart on the first hidden question. In interviews, the take-home round tests exactly this skill: expect 'walk me through your take-home: how did you keep test data out of the system?'

realWorld.title: Kapoor and Narayanan, 2023: the first kind of leakage
realWorld.text: The project page for their paper in Patterns lists, as the first kind of leakage, Lack of clean separation of training and test set. When the two are not kept apart at every step, it says, the model has access to information in the test set before its performance is evaluated. Nothing was trained here; the test answers reached the system at question time, through the index, which is the same failure at a later step.

realWorld.title: Kapoor and Narayanan: how common it is
realWorld.text: The same page reports: We find 41 papers from 30 fields where errors have been found, collectively affecting 648 papers. These are published studies, written and reviewed by experts, so a tired candidate at 05:00 is in large company.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: test the questions the documents can't answer
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to building evaluations lists example edge cases to include, among them Irrelevant or nonexistent input data. Question 18, the ski boots, is that kind of test: the right answer is that the documents don't say, and before the leak the assistant invented £35.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: success criteria should be measurable
realWorld.text: The same guide asks for criteria that are Measurable, and says: Use quantitative metrics or well-defined qualitative scales. Five chosen examples, the third reply, is neither: it has no count and no denominator.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.33: test information
realWorld.text: A third-party guide to the standard's Annex A control 8.33, Test Information, gives one of its purposes as: Selection of test information and the use of that information in order to obtain reliable results. That is the guide's wording, not the standard's; if you work to the standard, check the control in your own copy.

asked: Walk me through your take-home: how did you keep test data out of the system?
Your scores are on questions you wrote and tuned against. How should we read them?
interview.answer: I kept the test questions and their answers in a tests/ folder that nothing indexes, and I didn't rely on remembering that: the scorer runs a leak check first. It fails the run if any chunk in the index came from a test file, or if any test question matches a chunk at a similarity of 0.98 or more, because a near-perfect match usually means the answer itself is in there. In my case it caught a real leak: tidying up, I'd moved the answer file under the data folder, the re-index cut it into 20 chunks, and every answer copied its own row. Scores went to 20 of 20 right and faithful while recall@5, which only ranks document chunks, stayed 16. After the fix the honest numbers were 15 of 20 right, 17 faithful and recall@5 16, and I labelled them as questions I tuned on, because I'd been changing the system against those same 20. Read them as an upper bound. I listed the five failures, said what the numbers can't show, and the first next step is a fresh test set written before any more tuning. If I had more time, I'd also check for reworded copies, which a 0.98 threshold misses.

The storyteller's script that marks each answer against the answer key and counts right, faithful and recall@5, each out of 20.

atWork: Look for an eval set stored inside a folder your system reads. It is a common pattern: a team keeps test questions and their answers next to the documents, in the same bucket or folder, and a lookup index or an ingestion job picks them up. The first sign is usually a score that jumps for no reason, or answers that cite a file nobody meant to be a source. Ask four things. Where do the test questions and answers live, and can anything that builds the index read that place? Is there a check that fails if a chunk comes from a test file, or if a test question matches something in the index almost word for word? Which questions were used to tune the system, and are the reported numbers labelled that way? And is there a set written before the tuning, kept for the final number? Build Night: X2, Evals on 50 past incidents, has the same shape as this case's honest report: baseline and improved scores, each with its denominator and what it was measured on. It unlocks on a5e02, a5e03 and a5e04, not on this case. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 8.33 (test information, as summarised by third-party guides; check the wording in your own copy) is likely to expect test data to be chosen and kept so that results are reliable, and a leak check with a recorded result is evidence of that. Control A.8.29 is sometimes mapped here too, but it covers security testing in development and acceptance, not keeping test data apart. Building it into the scorer now costs far less than explaining a leaked answer file to an auditor later.

cards.title: Build Q&A plus an eval set

recall.prompt: A colleague's document assistant suddenly scores 48 of 48 on her test questions, up from 37 the day before. Her only change was tidying the project: she put qa.json, her questions with their right answers, into the folder the ingestion job reads. What happened, and what should she do before reporting?

keyIdeas.idea: The answer file was indexed, so each question found its own answer and the model copied it
Move the file out of anything indexed and add a check that fails on chunks from test files or near-exact matches
Report the earlier honest number, labelled as questions she tuned on, with the failures and a new set as the next step

recall.model: The tidy put her answer file where the ingestion job reads, so it was indexed: each question now finds its own answer almost word for word, and the model copies it. 48 of 48 measures the answer file, not the assistant; that's leakage. She should move the file out of anything indexed, re-run the indexing, and add a leak check that fails the run if any chunk comes from a test file or any question has a near-exact match. Then report the honest number, about 37 of 48, labelled as questions she tuned on, with the failures listed and a new set, written before more tuning, as the next step.

recall.prompt: After eval.csv was indexed, right and faithfulness went to 20 of 20, but recall@5 stayed at 16 of 20. Why?
options: Her recall check ranks only the 300 document chunks, so the answer rows never entered it
Recall@5 is always lower than faithfulness
The re-index didn't finish before the scorer ran
The four missed questions had no row in eval.csv
recall.why: The recall check asks whether the right document is in the top 5 of the chunks cut from the 50 documents. The 20 answer rows were never in that list, so it saw no change: 16 of 20. Right and faithful are judged on the answer, and the answer copied the row.

recall.prompt: An interviewer asks: walk me through your take-home. How did you keep test data out of the system, and how should we read your scores?

keyIdeas.idea: Test files live outside anything indexed, enforced by a check that fails the run
The check looks for chunks from test files and near-exact matches between test questions and the index
Scores on questions you tuned on are an upper bound; label them, show failures, and name a new set as the next step

recall.model: The test questions and answers live in a tests/ folder that nothing indexes, and the scorer runs a leak check before every run. It fails if any chunk came from a test file, or if any test question matches a chunk almost word for word, at a similarity of 0.98 or more. My numbers are on questions I tuned on, because I changed the system against them, so read them as an upper bound. I label them that way, list the failures, and the first next step is a new set written before any more tuning.

recall.prompt: 50 documents made 300 chunks. The indexer cuts a table one row per chunk. How many chunks does the index hold after eval.csv, with 20 rows, is moved under data/ and re-indexed?
recall.why: 300 document chunks + 20 rows, one chunk each = 320. Moving the file changes nothing until the re-index runs; at 04:30 the index still held 300.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Another company's take-home came on Thursday 4 February: 80 documents for a bike shop, 30 test questions to write. My leak check is now the first thing my scorer runs, and the answer file lives in tests/. This time it still failed: 0 chunks from tests/, but 12 of 30 questions match a chunk at 0.99. I had written those 12 by copying lines from the shop's frequently asked questions page, which is one of the 80 documents. My scorer says 27 of 30 right.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Is this a leak, and what should the report say?

keyIdeas.idea: Not the key leaking: the documents themselves hold those questions word for word, so they test copying, not finding
Rewrite those questions in a customer's own words, or write new ones without reading the FAQ
Report the two groups separately, each with its denominator, and say which were copied

coldCase.model: Not a leak of the key: the 12 questions match because the documents themselves hold them verbatim, so they test whether the search can find an exact copy, which is too easy. Rewrite them in a customer's own words, the way people actually ask, without reading the FAQ while you write. In the report, show the scores separately, out of 18 for the questions you wrote yourself and out of 12 for the copied ones, say which is which, and treat the 18 as the honest number.
